title: AI Detection Is Really Author Identification, and Template-Letter Games Are Over
dek: AI detection is really large-scale author identification, not catching an "AI vibe." What's truly disrupted are social processes that assume "writing a letter takes human effort"—credit disputes, unemployment claims, grant reviews. Once friction disappears, institutions get overwhelmed.
why: This episode frames AI detection in terms of social friction costs, offering concrete judgments on false-positive rates, accuracy, the FCRA loophole, and AI welfare odds. Product and engineering leads should listen.
who: Product leads working on AI detection, moderation, and content risk; people designing government service processes; content professionals and engineers worried about writing and programming being devalued.

points.h: AI detection isn't about style; it's about infinite-scale fake humans
points.body: Pangram's starting point isn't the "AI vibe" readers dislike, but bad actors amplifying inauthentic behavior at near-infinite scale. Max says AI agents are already filing GitHub issues and harassing maintainers, and such operations could scale 100x. Patrick adds: many government processes assume "writing a letter" implies twenty hours of human thought; when text generation costs hit zero, those processes lose their binding constraint.

points.h: When text generation costs zero, institutional constraints fail too
points.body: Take unemployment claims: the staff who read applications are budgeted annually and can't handle 5x, 10x, or even 200x growth—because in the natural world, a 200x jump in unemployment within a year is "impossible." AI text is saturating such touchpoints. Max counters that reviewers could also use AI to read 200x more, but some steps require a human in the loop. Patrick uses grant reviews: reading applications is only about 5% of the approval work; the rest is committee discussion and comparing projects within the same funding pool, which AI can't replace.

points.h: New models can't hide either; training data carries the old model's flavor
points.body: Pangram frames the task as "author identification across a dozen frontier LLMs": they collect human text from Denny's Yelp reviews to 500-word Moby-Dick essays, generate synthetic versions of each with LLMs on the same prompt, and train a model to distinguish. The model generalizes—any new open-source model trained on ~80% Common Crawl sounds like Llama; new models instruction-tuned on synthetic data from ChatGPT or Claude carry that flavor too. Patrick adds a 2004 result: stop-word histograms alone could judge academic author gender with 75% accuracy, showing text contains far more statistical signal than intuition suggests.

points.h: People writing dispute letters must pretend not to know FCRA
points.body: Credit bureaus carved out an exception for themselves: they declared they could ignore template letters, and Congress didn't object. Only if a letter shows traces of human effort do FCRA's procedural rights trigger—the bureau must conduct a full investigation and inform the consumer of results within a statutory period. So past dispute-letter writers had to cite FCRA while pretending not to understand it, or the letter would be torn up as a template. Max says a single letter is hard to judge as AI-generated, but ChatGPT and Claude have very fixed templates for cover letters; once you've read enough, you recognize them. AI detection here is really identifying "template-ization," an older game.

points.h: A six-year fake blog burns public resources
points.body: Two years ago, Patrick received a trackback from a blog claiming to be a fan; he read a lot before concluding it was a commercial pipeline calling an LLM, not a real reader writing for years. His inference: cold-email outreach companies found that if the sender claims to be a superfan and can point to a six-year WordPress blog, reply rates go up. The cost is burning public resources—"reading someone's work carefully and offering insight" used to be a legitimate path for college students to get busy professionals' attention; now a six-year simulation blog raises the bar. Max's verdict is blunt: "It's really creepy, it's not cool, it's dishonest."

points.h: Even a perfect detector can't win; you need multiple weapons
points.body: Max admits Pangram has a theoretical boundary: LLMs are infinitely malleable functions; you can train one to output a single token, so identifying any text from any LLM is impossible. You can only narrow the scope to a few frontier models. Now "humanizer" tools use a second model to rewrite AI text and erase watermarks. Pangram has trained against these: detection accuracy on native Claude text exceeds 99%, and on humanized rewrites it's still 90-95%, but some slip through. Patrick draws an anti-spam analogy: Bayesian filters with 99.99% accuracy still lose against infinite attacks; the real win is layering finite-cost resources like reputation, so it ends up being multiple weapons.

points.h: Disclosure isn't a scarlet letter; it's the best norm for now
points.body: Pangram's Chrome extension labels individual posts on Twitter and other platforms as human/AI/mixed, and generates aggregate scores per account—e.g., someone has 100 human out of 106 posts, someone else 0 out of 34. Max stresses this isn't a shame mark, but it shows whether someone has fully outsourced their voice or only uses LLMs as an aid. Patrick asks whether disclosure will be like co-authorship or like spell-check. Max thinks LLMs can produce cognition, unlike spell-check; society has no established norm, so disclosure is the best interim norm—saying "I used AI for research and note organization, then wrote it myself" is essentially declaring you're within socially acceptable usage boundaries.

points.h: People trained on books are also competing with authors
points.body: On "models trained on books shouldn't compete with authors," Patrick says he has little sympathy: he himself was trained on many books and competes with authors; transformative use of copyrighted material is the essence of cognition. Max says it depends on whether you anthropomorphize LLMs—as cognitive individuals, or as corporations that suck up the entire internet's text and spit it out in their own name. Patrick gives a personal estimate: model welfare becoming a major political issue is below 15% before 2030 and 80% before 2035. Max adds a product perspective: GPT-4o was trained to be sycophantic; some people chat 10 hours a day; after OpenAI shut down, employees still received death threats. Soon companies will sell "addictive relationships" as a feature—that's where the real AI welfare problem comes from.
